# A Secret Habit?

> "Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them."
>
> — Ephesians 5:11

Smoking was once a social habit. Men lit up together, offered the packet round, and stood about in doorways being companionable.

Nobody has ever said that about this one. You don't do it at a dinner party. It may be the most private thing you do, and that privacy is what keeps it going.

Your mind, your drive and your soul are the real reasons to stop, and they always were. You never needed a study to tell you so. The first week you did it as a boy, you locked the door. Nobody taught you to hide it. You knew.

## What the secret does {-}

**It makes every man think he's the only one.** You saw this with the church guy. A whole row of men, each sure the others are clean. If they compared notes for five minutes the spell would break.

**It protects the lies.** A lie kept in your head never has to face a question. Said aloud, it sounds as thin as it is. Try telling another grown man, with a straight face, "I need this in order to sleep."

**It splits you in two.** There's the man people meet, and the man behind the door, and the first spends a lot of energy making sure nobody meets the second. FitXFearless doesn't think the wall holds anyway: "the things you do in private come out in public". And C.S. Lewis, in the letter you read in the last chapter, saw what the wall does to the man behind it. For Lewis, "almost the main work of life is to come out of our selves, out of the little dark prison we are all born in." A secret is that prison with the bolt on the inside.

A man with a secret can't be fully known. A man who can't be fully known can't be fully trusted, and he never feels fully loved, because he's always thinking, "You wouldn't say that if you knew."

## The silence is cracking {-}

Something has shifted in the last fifteen years. There was a time when a man might boast about how often. Today more than a million men have joined forums to talk about stopping. Today's strong man doesn't want to be led about by an itch.

Those forums have done real good. A man logs on and finds out he was never the only one. But the method they hand him is nearly always willpower: counters, badges, resets, and a great deal of gritted teeth. They shut the door and leave the desire in the room, so the mood is often self-pity where it ought to be joy. Those men are falling forward, though, and their effort isn't wasted.

This book works the other way round. It removes the desire first. The door then closes without anyone having to lean on it.

## Into the light {-}

Here is how Paul goes on: "For it is a shame even to speak of the things which are done by them in secret. But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light" (Ephesians 5:12–13).

In the dark this habit looks big, and it looks like yours alone. In the light it's a small, dull thing that millions of men do, for no gain at all.

You've been bringing it into the light since page one. Every chapter has taken one more piece of it out and looked at it. That's why it's shrinking.

Heath Lambert draws a line worth remembering: "Godly sorrow doesn't fear that people will find out about your sin." The dread of being found out isn't repentance. It's the habit guarding itself.

Whether to tell another person, and whom, comes later in the book. For now, do one thing. Stop hiding it from yourself, and stop hiding it from God. He has seen every time, and he hasn't left. If you're an atheist, play along: say the plain facts aloud in an empty room, and notice how much smaller they sound.

Every day more men walk out into the light. The ones left behind get more afraid of being the last.

**DON'T BE THE LAST MAN IN THE DARK.**
